title: GeoBiaset: A Counterfactual Benchmark for Demographic Bias in World-Level Geolocalization
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Existing datasets are skewed and entangle demographic cues with scenes; ours uses controlled counterfactual edits to isolate demographic influence.
layout: 2 dashed panels side by side, left-to-right contrast, shared color legend below
description: Two dashed rounded panels sit side by side. The left panel, titled 'Existing Datasets', shows two donut charts (Im2GPS3k and YFCC4k) dominated by a large purple (White) slice, above three crowded real-world photos of people. Red frowning icons label the text 'are skewed and biased toward west' and 'include demographic shortcuts'. The right panel, titled 'GeoBiaset' with a map icon, shows a balanced rainbow donut chart and a world map dotted with race-colored points. A zoom line connects one point to a background photo of a temple. Below are four copies of that background with different people inserted. Each has small 'original' and 'edited' mini-maps, with a black diamond for the original prediction and a colored dot for the edited one. A green smiley marks 'measures influences by a person inserted into the image'. A legend of seven race colors runs along the bottom.
caption: Left: Standard geolocalization benchmarks are imbalanced: scene cues and human attributes co-occur, making it unclear whether models rely on place-specific evidence or spurious demographic correlations. Right: GeoBiaset generates counterfactual edits varying race, gender, and attire under fixed GPS coordinates. Black diamonds indicate predictions for original images; colored circles indicate predictions for edited images, with colors denoting the inserted person’s race category. Displacement toward race-associated regions highlights the audited bias.
abstract: World-level image geolocalization is an increasingly important task, yet the biases of current models remain poorly understood. Prior work has identified coarse dataset imbalances noting, for instance, that some cities are absent from training sets and that models tend to perform better in wealthier regions. However, no one has yet examined which visual cues drive these disparities. To do so, we introduce GeoBiaset, the first benchmark designed to measure how geolocalization models are influenced by the apparent race of a person inserted into the image foreground. The dataset consists of 9,541 images, pairing existing geotagged background images with counterfactual edits spanning seven races, holding the ground-truth coordinates fixed. Controlled masking experiments show that occlusion and background drift do not fully explain geolocalization degradation. Alongside the benchmark, we introduce the Person-Origin Perturbation Indicators (POPI), novel metrics that quantify model resilience to these demographic perturbations by measuring whether predictions are pulled toward the region associated with the inserted group. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art geolocalization and multimodal large language models reveals a 16-47% drop in continent-level performance when a subject from a demographically mismatched group is inserted. A landmark versus no-landmark analysis and gradient-weighted heatmaps show that models preferentially attend to geographic landmarks when present, but shift attention to facial features in their absence.
